title: How Much Can Change?
principle: Change inside a group is easy to see.

t: Everyone agrees animals change. Nobody argues about that. The argument is about how far.
Both sides of this whole disagreement accept that populations change, that new species appear, and that selection is real. The dispute is entirely about the ceiling.
sub: So this lesson is about where people think the ceiling is.
Naming the actual point of disagreement is most of the work. It is not where most arguments about this assume it is.

t: Run the beetles again. Watch how far they can get, and then watch them stop.
Run the beetles again with a very dark ground. Notice that they change fast at first and then stop changing — and ask yourself what ran out.
goal: They got there — and then they stopped. There was nothing left to pick from.
The population reached the ground shade and then went flat. Selection can only work on differences that exist; once they are used up, it has nothing to act on.

question: Selection uses up the variation it acts on. So where does new variation come from?
Selection depletes the variance it acts upon. What replenishes it, and is that source sufficient?
options: New mutations, copying errors and gene duplication
stages.outcome: New mutations, copying errors and gene duplication
note: Commit. This is the exact hinge of the dispute: everyone agrees selection depletes variation, and everyone agrees mutation supplies some. The question is whether it supplies enough, and of the right kind.

t: Change inside a group is easy to see. Change into a whole new kind of thing is the argument.
Small-scale change within a population is directly observed. Whether the same process, given enough time, accounts for the major groups is what is actually disputed.

Microevolution — change in allele frequencies within populations, including speciation — is observed and undisputed. Macroevolution — the origin of major body plans by the same mechanism extrapolated — is the contested extrapolation.

The terms are worth using precisely, because a great deal of argument at cross purposes comes from one side defending observed microevolution and the other attacking unobserved macroevolution, as though the same claim were in view.
sub: Both sides agree new species can appear. That surprises most people.
Speciation is accepted by both sides. So is natural selection. So is mutation.
Creationist biology accepts speciation and in fact requires it to run rapidly, since it must derive today's species from a limited number of ancestral kinds within a few thousand years.

The creationist model requires diversification rates that exceed mainstream estimates by orders of magnitude, which is a rarely-noticed feature of the disagreement: it is not a dispute about whether populations change quickly.

t: Here is what each side says about the ceiling, and why.
The disagreement is about whether an observed small-scale process extrapolates. Open both.
evidence: Everyone agrees on the observations: species do appear, mutations do happen, and selection does work.

Agreed on all sides: new species arise, mutation generates novel sequence, gene duplication occurs, and selection acts. Laboratory instances — nylon-digesting enzymes, citrate use arising in Lenski's long-term E. coli experiment, antibiotic resistance — are accepted as real by both.

claim: There is no ceiling. Enough small changes, given enough time, add up to big ones.
There is no known barrier. The same processes, extended over deep time, account for the major groups.
because: Mutation keeps making new differences, and gene copying means a spare copy can be changed into something new without breaking the original.

Gene duplication supplies raw material that can diverge without cost to the original function, and duplication-and-divergence is documented in real gene families — the globins, the opsins that give colour vision. No mechanism has been proposed that would halt accumulated change at any particular level, and the fossil, anatomical and genetic patterns converge on the same tree.
predicts: New examples of new abilities appearing should keep turning up in the lab.
Novel functions should continue to be observed arising and to be traceable to duplication, recombination or mutation; and no principled boundary should be found where change stops.

claim: There is a ceiling. Creatures vary a lot inside their created kind, and not past it.
Variation is bounded. Diversification occurs freely within an originally created kind but does not cross between kinds.
because: The changes we actually watch are mostly things breaking or being lost, or shuffling what was already there — not brand new instructions appearing.

They argue observed cases typically involve loss or degradation of existing function, regulatory change, or recombination of pre-existing variation rather than genuinely novel specified information, and cite Behe's survey of laboratory evolution to that effect. Sanford's genetic entropy argument adds that deleterious mutations accumulate faster than selection removes them, which would set a limit in the opposite direction from the one usually discussed.
predicts: Studying the famous examples closely should keep showing something was lost or reused, not newly built.

Close analysis of novel functions should continue to reveal loss, duplication of pre-existing information, or regulatory switching; and mutation-accumulation studies should show fitness decline over generations.

ask: What would 'brand new instructions' actually look like, so you could tell if you found some?

The argument turns on a term neither side has fully pinned down: new information. Before deciding who is right, ask what measurement would settle whether a given change added information — and notice that until that is specified, both sides can describe the same experiment as supporting them. That is a sign the question needs sharpening rather than more evidence.

q: What do both sides of this argument actually agree about?
Which of these is agreed by both accounts?
Which claim is common ground across the dispute?
options: That natural selection is real and new species appear
That all life shares one ancestor
why: Natural selection is not the argument. Both sides think it happens. The argument is about how far it can take you.
Selection, mutation and speciation are common ground. Finding the actual point of disagreement — the ceiling — is what makes it possible to argue about the right thing.

Locating the genuine locus of dispute is a discipline worth having in every argument, not only this one. Most heat here is generated by attacking positions the other side does not hold: selection and speciation are accepted on both accounts, and universal common descent is the contested claim.

t: Working out exactly what someone disagrees with you about is most of the argument.

The habit generalises well beyond biology: before disputing a claim, state the strongest version of it and identify precisely which step you reject. Arguments that skip that step tend to run for decades without either side landing a blow.
